fields.title: Union and Communion
fields.subtitle: Thoughts on the Song of Solomon
fields.description: Hudson Taylor’s meditations on the Song of Solomon, tracing the soul’s progress from first communion with Christ into deep and unbroken union with Him. Written by the founder of the China Inland Mission, it is a brief but searching guide to intimacy with the Lord.

fields.title: Foreword
fields.body_html:
This little book sets out to lead the devout Bible student into the Green Pastures of the Good Shepherd, from there to the Banqueting House of the King, and from there to work in the Vineyard. It is one of the lasting gifts Mr. Hudson Taylor left to the Church. With an evident anointing from the Holy One, he was able to open up, in the simplest language, the deep truth of the believer’s personal union with the Lord, which is the subject of The Song of Songs under its symbols and images. In doing so he has given reliable guidance on one of the most commonly neglected and misunderstood books of Scripture. How many have been bewildered by its rich language and its wealth of imagery, which both hide and reveal its meaning, and have said, “How can I understand except some man should guide me?” It is safe to say that these pages cannot fail to help and bless all such readers.

For those who knew him, Mr. Hudson Taylor’s life underlined the value of this small volume. What he explains here, he also lived. If his words point to the possibility and the blessedness of union with Christ, his whole life showed it in actual experience. He lived as one who was “married to Another, even to Him Who is raised from the dead”; and out of that union he brought forth “fruit unto God.” Who he was gives his words here a meaning and a confirmation that can hardly be overstated. Inevitably some will read this and dismiss it as mystical and impractical, because it deals so directly with the intimacies of fellowship with the unseen Lord. I would, however, venture to remind them that the writer of these pages founded the China Inland Mission! He turned his vision of the Beloved into a lifetime of strenuous service, and so kept it bright through all the years of a life that has hardly had an equal in our own day.

This is really what commends the short chapters that follow. They proclaim good news distilled from experience, and at the very least they mark out a path through this enclosed part of God’s Word that will lead many who walk it into the joys of Emmanuel’s land.

J. STUART HOLDEN

ST. PAUL’S,

PORTMAN SQUARE, LONDON W.

June 1, 1914.

fields.title: Introductory
fields.body_html:
The great purpose toward which all God’s dealings through the ages are moving is revealed to us in the fifteenth chapter of Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians: “That God may be all in all.” Our Lord’s teaching in John 17:3 agrees with this: “And this is (the object of) life eternal, that they might know Thee the only true God, and JESUS CHRIST, whom Thou hast sent.” If this is so, would it not be wise to keep this goal always in view in our daily life and in our study of God’s holy Word?

All Scripture is given by inspiration of God and is profitable, so no part of it is, or can be, neglected without loss. Few parts of the Word will help the devout student more in pursuing this all-important “knowledge of God” than the much-neglected “Song of Solomon.” Like other parts of God’s Word, this book has its difficulties. But so do all the works of God. Is not the very fact that they are beyond our unaided understanding and research a “sign-manual,” a signature, of their divinity? Can feeble human beings expect to grasp divine power, or to understand and interpret the works and providences of the All-wise? And if not, is it surprising that His Word also needs more than human wisdom to interpret it? Thanks be to God, the light of the HOLY GHOST is promised to all who seek it: what more could we want?

Read without the key, this book is especially hard to understand, but the key is easily found in the plain teaching of the New Testament. The Incarnate Word is the true key to the written Word. Yet even before the incarnation, a devout student of the Old Testament would have found much help in understanding the sacred mysteries of this book in the prophets, for there Israel was taught that her MAKER was her HUSBAND. John the Baptist, the last of the prophets, recognized the Bridegroom in the person of CHRIST, and said, “He that hath the bride is the Bridegroom: but the friend of the Bridegroom, which standeth and heareth Him, rejoiceth greatly because of the Bridegroom’s voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled.” In the fifth chapter of Ephesians Paul goes further still, teaching that the union of CHRIST with His Church, and her submission to Him, lies beneath the very relationship of marriage and gives the pattern for every godly union.

In Solomon, the bridegroom king and also the author of this poem, we have a picture of our LORD, the true Prince of peace, in His coming reign. Then there will be not only His bride, the Church, but also a willing people, His subjects, over whom He will reign in glory. Then distant rulers will bring their wealth and see the glory of the enthroned KING, testing Him with hard questions, as the Queen of Sheba once came to King Solomon; and blessed will they be who are given this privilege. A brief glimpse will be enough for them for a lifetime. But what will be the royal dignity and blessedness of the risen and exalted bride! Forever with her LORD, forever like her LORD, forever aware that His desire is toward her, she will share both His heart and His throne. Can studying a book that helps us understand these mysteries of grace and love be anything but deeply profitable?

It is interesting to notice the contrast between this book and the one before it. The Book of Ecclesiastes teaches emphatically that “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity”: and so it forms the necessary introduction to the Song of Solomon, which shows how true blessing and satisfaction are found. In the same way our SAVIOUR’S teaching in John 4 shows in a word that earthly things cannot give lasting satisfaction, in striking contrast to the flow of blessing that comes from the presence of the HOLY GHOST (whose work is not to reveal Himself but to reveal CHRIST as the Bridegroom of the soul): “Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again; but whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst: but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up”—overflowing, on and on—“unto everlasting life.”

We will find it helpful to look at the book in six sections:—

  • I. The Unsatisfied Life and its Remedy.
  • Chapter i. 2-ii. 7.
  • II. Communion Broken. Restoration.
  • Chapter ii. 8-iii. 5.
  • III. Unbroken Communion.
  • Chapter iii. 6-v. 1.
  • IV. Communion Again Broken. Restoration
  • Chapter v. 2-vi. 10.
  • V. Fruits of Recognized Union.
  • Chapter vi. 11-viii. 4.
  • VI. Unrestrained Communion.
  • Chapter viii. 5-14.

In each of these sections the speakers are the bride, the Bridegroom, and the daughters of Jerusalem. It is not usually hard to tell who is speaking, though people have reached different conclusions about some of the verses. The bride speaks of the Bridegroom as “her Beloved”; the Bridegroom speaks of her as “His love”; and the daughters of Jerusalem address her in more varied ways. In the last four sections they call her “the fairest among women,” but in the fifth she is called “the Shulamite,” or the King’s bride, and also the “Prince’s daughter.”

Anyone studying this book will find it a great help to mark their Bible carefully. A horizontal line marking off each speech, with a double line dividing the sections, would be useful, as would vertical lines in the margin to show who is speaking. We ourselves have ruled a single line to join the verses that contain the bride’s words, a double line for the Bridegroom’s, and a wavy line for the words of the daughters of Jerusalem.

Notice that the bride is the main speaker in Sections I and II, and is much taken up with herself. But in Section III, where the communion is unbroken, she has little to say and appears as the listener; the daughters of Jerusalem give a long speech, and the Bridegroom gives His longest. In that section He calls her His bride for the first time, and draws her into fellowship in service. In Section IV the bride is again the main speaker, but after she is restored the Bridegroom speaks at length, and “upbraideth not.” In Section V, as we noted, the bride is no longer called “the fairest among women,” but she claims to be, and is recognized as, the royal bride. In Section VI the Bridegroom claims her from her very birth, and not only from her betrothal, as GOD claimed Israel in Ezekiel 16.

In the secret of His presence

How my soul delights to hide!

Oh, how precious are the lessons

Which I learn at JESUS’ side!

Earthly cares can never vex me,

Neither trials lay me low;

For when Satan comes to vex me,

To the secret place I go!

fields.title: The Title
fields.body_html:
“The Song of Songs, which is Solomon’s.”

Well may this book be called the Song of Songs! There is no song like it. Read rightly, it brings a gladness to the heart that is as far above the joy of earthly things as heaven is above the earth. It has been well said that this is a song that only grace can teach and only experience can learn. Our SAVIOUR, speaking of the union of the branch with the vine, adds, “These things have I spoken unto you, that My joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full” (John 15:11). And the beloved disciple, writing of Him who “was from the beginning,” who “was with the FATHER, and was manifested unto us,” so that we might share the fellowship He enjoyed, also says, “These things we write unto you, that your joy may be full.” Union with CHRIST and abiding in CHRIST: what do they not secure? Peace, perfect peace; rest, constant rest; answers to all our prayers; victory over all our enemies; pure, holy living; ever-increasing fruitfulness. All of these, every one, are the glad result of abiding in CHRIST. The practical use of this precious Book is to deepen this union and to make this abiding more constant.

fields.title: Section I
fields.body_html:
THE UNSATISFIED LIFE AND ITS REMEDY

Song 1:2–2:7

It is easy to recognize the bride as the speaker in verses 2–7. These are not the words of someone dead in trespasses and sins, to whom the LORD is like a root out of dry ground, without form or beauty. The speaker has had her eyes opened to see His beauty, and she longs to enjoy His love more fully.

Let Him kiss me with the kisses of His mouth:

For Thy love is better than wine.

It is good that it should be so; it marks a distinct stage in the growth of the life of grace in the soul. And this recorded experience gives, as it were, Divine permission to long for felt signs of His presence, for felt tokens of His love. It was not always like this for her. Once she was content when He was away; other company and other occupations were enough for her. But now it can never be like that again. The world can never be to her what it once was; the betrothed bride has learned to love her LORD, and no company but His can satisfy her. His visits may be occasional and brief, but they are precious times of joy. She treasures their memory in between and longs for them to come again. There is no real satisfaction when He is away, and yet, sadly, He is not always with her: He comes and goes. One moment her joy in Him is heaven on earth; the next she is longing, and longing in vain, for His presence. Like the ever-changing tide, her experience ebbs and flows; it may even be that restlessness is the rule and satisfaction the exception. Is there no help for this? Must it always go on like this? Has He, could He have, created these longings that cannot be quenched only to tease them? That would be strange indeed. Yet are there not many of the LORD’S people whose usual experience is just like hers? They do not know the rest and joy of abiding in CHRIST; they do not know how to reach it, or why it is not theirs. Are there not many who look back to the delightful days when they were first betrothed to Him, and who, far from finding a richer inheritance in CHRIST now than they had then, are even aware that they have lost their first love? They might put their experience in the sad lament:—

Where is the blessedness I knew

When first I saw the Lord?

Others, who may not have lost their first love, may still feel that the occasional breaks in communion are becoming more and more unbearable, as the world means less to them and He means more. His absence is a growing distress. “Oh that I knew where I might find Him!” “Let Him kiss me with the kisses of His mouth: for Thy love is better than wine.” If only His love were strong and constant like mine, and He never withdrew the light of His face!”

Poor mistaken one! There is a love far stronger than yours waiting and longing to be satisfied. The Bridegroom is waiting for you all the time; the conditions that keep Him from coming near are all of your own making. Take the right place before Him, and He will be most ready, most glad, to “Satisfy thy deepest longings, to meet, supply thine every need.” What would we think of a betrothed woman whose pride and self-will stood in the way not only of her own complete joy but of the joy of the one who had given her his heart? She is never at rest when he is away, yet she cannot trust him fully; and she is unwilling to give up her own name, her own rights and possessions, and her own will to the one who has become necessary to her happiness. She would like to claim him fully without giving herself fully to him; but it can never be. As long as she keeps her own name, she can never claim his. She may not promise to love and honour if she will not also promise to obey; and until her love reaches that point of surrender she must remain an unsatisfied lover. She cannot, as a satisfied bride, find rest in her husband’s home. As long as she keeps her own will and control of her own possessions, she must be content to live on her own resources; she cannot claim his.

Could there be a sadder proof of how far-reaching and real the Fall is than the deep-seated distrust of our loving LORD and MASTER that makes us hesitate to give ourselves entirely to Him? We fear that He might ask for something beyond our strength, or call for something we would find hard to give or do. The real secret of an unsatisfied life is too often an unsurrendered will. And yet how foolish this is, as well as how wrong! Do we imagine we are wiser than He is? Or that our love for ourselves is more tender and strong than His? Or that we know ourselves better than He does? How our distrust must grieve and wound again the tender heart of Him who became for us the Man of Sorrows! How would an earthly bridegroom feel if he discovered that his bride-to-be dreaded marrying him, in case, once he had the power, he made her life unbearable? Yet how many of the LORD’S redeemed people treat Him in just this way! No wonder they are neither happy nor satisfied!

But true love cannot stand still; it must either decline or grow. In spite of all the unworthy fears of our poor hearts, Divine love is bound to win. The bride exclaims:—

Thine ointments have a goodly fragrance;

Thy name is as ointment poured forth;

Therefore do the virgins love Thee.

There was no ointment like the one with which the High Priest was anointed, and our Bridegroom is a Priest as well as a King. The trembling bride cannot entirely set aside her fears, but the restlessness and the longing become unbearable, and she resolves to surrender everything and, whatever happens, to follow Him fully. She will give her very self to Him, heart and hand, influence and possessions. Nothing could be as unbearable as His absence! If He leads her to another Moriah, or even to a Calvary, she will follow Him.

Draw me: we will run after Thee!

But what follows? A wonderfully glad surprise. No Moriah, no Calvary; instead, a KING! When the heart submits, JESUS reigns. And when JESUS reigns, there is rest.

And where does He lead His bride?

The King hath brought me into His chambers.

Not first to the banqueting house; that will come in due time. First, she is brought to be alone with Him.

How perfect! Could we be satisfied to meet someone we love only in public? No; we want to take that person aside and have them all to ourselves. So it is with our MASTER. He takes His now fully consecrated bride aside, to taste and enjoy the sacred intimacies of His wonderful love. The Bridegroom of His Church longs for communion with His people more than they long for fellowship with Him, and often has to cry:—

Let Me see thy countenance, let Me hear thy voice;

For sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.

Are we not all too ready to seek Him because of our own need rather than for His joy and pleasure? This should not be so. We do not admire selfish children who think only of what they can get from their parents and give no thought to the pleasure they might give or the help they might offer. But are we not in danger of forgetting that pleasing GOD means giving Him pleasure? Some of us can remember when the words “To please GOD” meant no more to us than not sinning against Him, not grieving Him. But would earthly parents’ love be satisfied with the mere absence of disobedience? Or would a bridegroom, if his bride sought him only to supply her own needs?

A word about the morning watch may be in place here. No time is spent so profitably as the early hour given to JESUS alone. Do we give this hour enough attention? If at all possible, it should be won back; nothing can make up for it. We must take time to be holy! One more thought. When we bring our questions to GOD, do we not sometimes go straight on to another request, or leave our place of prayer without waiting for His answers? Does this not show that we expect little in the way of an answer, and want little? Would we like to be treated like that? Quietly waiting before GOD would spare us many a mistake and many a sorrow.

We have found the bride making the glad discovery of a KING, her KING, and not the cross she expected. This is the first fruit of her consecration.

We will be glad and rejoice in Thee,

We will make mention of Thy love more than of wine.

Rightly do they love Thee.

Another discovery, no less important, is waiting for her. She has seen the face of the KING, and just as the rising sun shows what was hidden in the darkness, so His light has shown her own blackness to her. “Ah,” she cries, “I am black”;—“But comely,” the Bridegroom breaks in, with matchless grace and tenderness. “No, ‘black as the tents of Kedar,’” she goes on. “Yet to Me,” He answers, “you are ‘comely as the curtains of Solomon!’” Nothing humbles the soul like sacred and intimate communion with the Lord; yet there is a sweet joy in knowing that He knows everything, and still loves us all the same. Things we once called “little negligences” are seen with new eyes in “the secret of His presence.” There we see the mistake, the sin, of not keeping our own vineyard. The bride confesses this:—

Look not upon me, because I am swarthy,

Because the sun hath scorched me.

My mother’s sons were incensed against me,

They made me keeper of the vineyards;

But mine own vineyard have I not kept.

Our attention is drawn here to a danger that belongs above all to our own day. The intense activity of our times may lead to zeal in service at the cost of personal communion; but that neglect will not only lessen the value of the service, it will tend to unfit us for the highest service. If we watch over the souls of others and neglect our own, if we try to remove the specks from our brother’s eye while ignoring the log in our own, we will often be disappointed at how powerless we are to help our brothers and sisters, and our MASTER will be no less disappointed in us. Let us never forget that what we are matters more than what we do, and that all fruit borne while not abiding in CHRIST must be fruit of the flesh and not of the SPIRIT. The sin of neglected communion may be forgiven and yet its effect remain for good, just as a healed wound often leaves a scar.

We now come to a very sweet sign that the bride’s heart is truly united with her LORD. She is one with the GOOD SHEPHERD, and her heart at once goes out by instinct to feeding the flock. But she wants to walk in the footsteps of the One her soul loves, and she will neither work alone nor in any company but His:—

Tell me, O Thou whom my soul loveth,

Where Thou feedest Thy flock, where Thou makest it to rest at noon:

For why should I be as one that is veiled

Beside the flocks of Thy companions?

She will not mistake the company of His servants for the company of their MASTER.

If thou know not, O thou fairest among women,

Go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock,

And feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents.

These are the words of the daughters of Jerusalem, and they give a right answer to her questions. Let her show her love for her LORD by feeding His sheep and caring for His lambs (see John 21:15–17), and she need not fear missing His presence. While she shares with other under-shepherds in caring for His flock, she will find the CHIEF SHEPHERD at her side and enjoy the signs of His approval. It will be service with JESUS as well as for JESUS.

But far sweeter than the reply of the daughters of Jerusalem is the voice of the Bridegroom, who now speaks for Himself. It is the living fruit of her heart’s oneness with Him that makes His love break out in the joyful words of verses 9–11. For it is not only true that our love for our LORD will show itself in feeding His sheep. It is also true that He who said on earth, “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these My brethren, ye have done it unto Me,” has His own heart’s love stirred, and often reveals Himself in a special way to those who are serving Him.

The praise of the bride in verse 9 is strikingly fitting and beautiful:—

I have compared thee, O My love,

To a company of horses in Pharaoh’s chariots.

Remember that horses originally came out of Egypt, and that the pure breed still found in Arabia was brought by Solomon’s merchants, during his reign, for all the kings of the East. The horses chosen for Pharaoh’s own chariot would not only be of the purest blood and perfectly proportioned, but also perfectly trained, gentle and obedient. They would know no will but the charioteer’s, and the only purpose of their existence would be to carry the king wherever he wanted to go. So it should be with the Church of CHRIST: one body with many members, lived in and guided by one SPIRIT, holding fast to the HEAD and knowing no will but His. Her swift and harmonious movement should carry His kingdom forward throughout the world.

Many years ago a dear friend, returning from the East by the overland route, made the journey from Suez to Cairo in the clumsy stagecoach then in use. When the passengers had landed and taken their seats, about a dozen wild young horses were harnessed to the coach with ropes. The driver took his seat and cracked his whip, and the horses dashed off, some to the right, some to the left, and others forward. The coach started with a jolt and stopped just as suddenly, first throwing those in the front seat into the laps of those behind, and then the other way round. With enough Arabs running on each side to keep these wild animals heading in the right direction, the passengers were jerked and jolted, bruised and shaken, until by the time they reached their destination they were too tired and sore to get the rest they badly needed.

Is the Church of GOD today not more like these untrained horses than a company of horses in Pharaoh’s chariot? And while self-will and division are plain to see in the Church, can we be surprised that the world still lies in the power of the wicked one, and that the great heathen nations have barely been touched?

Changing His picture, the Bridegroom goes on:—

Thy cheeks are comely with plaits of hair,

Thy neck with strings of jewels.

We will make thee plaits of gold

With studs of silver.

The bride is not only beautiful and useful to her LORD; she is also adorned, and He delights to add to her ornaments. His gifts are not flowers that fade or trinkets of no real worth. The finest gold, the purest silver, and the most precious and lasting jewels are the Royal Bridegroom’s gifts to His bride; and when they are braided into her own hair they add to the pleasure of the One who gave them.

In verses 12–14 the bride answers:—

While the King sat at His table

My spikenard sent forth its fragrance.

It is in His presence and by His grace that whatever fragrance or beauty there may be in us comes out. All that is gracious and divine is from Him as its source, through Him as its instrument, and to Him as its end. But HE HIMSELF is far better than everything His grace works in us.

My Beloved is unto me as a bundle of myrrh,

That lieth betwixt my breasts.

My beloved is unto me as a cluster of henna-flowers

In the vineyards of En-gedi.

It is good when our eyes are filled with His beauty and our hearts are taken up with Him. To the extent that this is true of us, we will recognize the matching truth that His great heart is taken up with us. Notice the Bridegroom’s response:—

Behold, thou art fair, My love; behold, thou art fair;

Thine eyes are as a dove’s.

How can the Bridegroom truthfully use such words of one who recognizes herself as

Black as the tents of Kedar?

And the Bridegroom’s words in chapter 4:7 are stronger still:—

Thou art all fair, My love;

And there is no spot in thee.

We will find the answer to this difficulty in 2 Corinthians 3. As Moses gazed on the Divine glory he was so transformed that the Israelites could not look at the glory of his face. “We all, with unveiled face (beholding and) reflecting as a mirror the glory of the LORD, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory (i.e. the brightness caught from His glory transforms us to glory), even as from the LORD the SPIRIT.” Every mirror has two sides. One is dull, reflects nothing, and is all spots; but when the reflecting side is turned toward us, we see no spot, only our own image. So while the bride delights in the Bridegroom’s beauty, He sees His own image in her. There is no spot in that: it is all fair. May we always hold up this reflection to His gaze, and to the world we live in for the very purpose of reflecting Him.

Notice His words again:—

Thine eyes are as dove’s,

or

Thou hast dove’s eyes.

The hawk is a beautiful bird with beautiful eyes, quick and piercing; but the Bridegroom does not want hawk’s eyes in His bride. The gentle eyes of the innocent dove are the ones He admires. It was as a dove that the HOLY SPIRIT came upon Him at His baptism, and the character of the dove is what He looks for in each of His people.

The reason David was not allowed to build the Temple is very significant. His life was far from perfect, and the HOLY SPIRIT has faithfully recorded his mistakes and sins. They brought God’s discipline on him. Yet none of these disqualified him from building the Temple; it was his warlike spirit, even though many of his battles, if not all, were fought to establish GOD’S Kingdom and fulfil His promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Only Solomon, the Prince of Peace, could build the Temple. If we want to win souls and build up the Church, which is His Temple, let us take note: it is not by debate or argument, but by lifting up CHRIST, that we will draw people to Him.

Now we come to the bride’s reply. He has called her fair, and she answers wisely and well:—

Behold Thou art fair, my Beloved, yea, pleasant:

Also our couch is green.

The beams of our house are cedars,

And our rafters are firs.

I am (but) a rose of Sharon,

A lily of the valleys.

The last words are often quoted as though the Bridegroom spoke them, but we believe this is mistaken. In effect the bride is saying: You call me fair and pleasant, but the fairness and pleasantness are Yours. I am only a wild flower, a lowly, scentless rose of Sharon (that is, the autumn crocus), or a lily of the valley.

To this the Bridegroom replies: “So be it; but if a wild flower, yet

As a lily among thorns,

So is My love among the daughters.”

Again the bride answers:—

As the apple tree (the citron) among the trees of the wood,

So is my Beloved among the sons.

I sat down under His shadow with great delight,

And His fruit was sweet to my taste.

The citron is a beautiful evergreen that gives delightful shade as well as refreshing fruit. A humble wild flower herself, she sees her Bridegroom as a noble tree, both beautiful and fruitful. In Him she finds shade from the burning sun, refreshment and rest. What a contrast between where she is now, and how she feels, and the way this section began! He knew perfectly well the cause of all her fears. Her distrust came from not knowing Him, so He took her aside, and in the sweet intimacies of shared love her fears and distrust have vanished like morning mist before the rising sun.

But now that she has come to know Him, she experiences His love in a further way. He is not ashamed to acknowledge her in public.

He brought me to the banqueting house,

And His banner over me was love.

The house of wine is now as fitting as the King’s chambers were before. Without fear or shame she can sit at His side, His acknowledged wife, the bride of His choice. Overwhelmed by His love, she exclaims:—

Stay ye me with raisins, comfort me with apples:

For I am sick of love.

His left hand is under my head,

And His right hand doth embrace me.

Now she discovers the blessedness of belonging to Him. No longer her own, she has rest of heart as both her right and her joy; and that is how the Bridegroom wants it.

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem,

By the roes, and by the hinds of the field,

That ye stir not up nor awake My love,

Until she please.

It is never His will that our rest in Him should be disturbed.

You may always be abiding,

If you will, at Jesus’ side;

in the secret of His presence

You may every moment hide.

There is no change in His love; He is the same yesterday, today, and forever. To us He promises, “I will never leave thee, never fail thee, nor forsake thee”; and His earnest appeal and command is, “Abide in Me, and I in you.”

fields.title: Section II
fields.body_html:
Communion Broken—Restoration

Song 2:8–3:5

“Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things that were heard, lest haply we drift away from them.”—Heb. ii. 1 (R.V.).

At the end of the first section we left the bride satisfied and at rest in the arms of her Beloved, who had charged the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken His love until she pleased. We might suppose that a union so complete and a satisfaction so full would never be broken by any failure on the happy bride’s part. But sadly, the experience of most of us shows how easily communion with CHRIST can be broken, and how much we need our LORD’S urging to abide in Him, urging addressed to those who truly are branches of the true Vine and have been made clean by the Word He has spoken. The failure is never on His side. “Lo, I am with you alway.” But the bride, alas, often forgets the appeal made to her in Psalm 45:—

Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear;

Forget also thine own people, and thy father’s house;

So shall the King greatly desire thy beauty;

For He is thy Lord; and worship thou Him.

In this section the bride has drifted back from her place of blessing into worldliness. Perhaps the very restfulness of her newfound joy made her feel too secure. Perhaps she thought that, as far as she was concerned, there was no need for the warning, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.” Or she may have thought that the love of the world had been so completely taken away that she could safely go back, and that by a little compromise on her part she might win her friends to follow her LORD too. Perhaps she hardly thought at all. Glad to be saved and free, she forgot that the current, the course of this world, was against her, and without noticing she glided and drifted back to the very place she had been called out of, unaware all the while that she was backsliding. When the current is against us, we do not need to turn the boat downstream in order to drift; and a runner in a race does not need to turn back in order to miss the prize.

How often the enemy succeeds, by one trick or another, in tempting the believer away from that complete consecration to CHRIST in which alone the fullness of His power and love can be experienced. We say the fullness of His power and love, for the believer may not have stopped loving the LORD. In the passage before us the bride still loves Him truly, though not wholly. There is still a power in His Word that she feels, though she no longer obeys at once. She hardly realizes how she is wronging her LORD, or how real the wall between them is. To her, worldliness seems a small thing. She has not grasped the solemn truth of many passages in God’s Word that speak in the strongest terms of the folly, the danger and the sin of friendship with the world. “Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the FATHER is not in him.” “Ye adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with GOD? Whosoever therefore would be a friend of the world maketh himself an enemy of GOD.” “Be not unequally yoked with unbelievers; for what fellowship have righteousness and iniquity? or what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath CHRIST with Belial? or what portion hath a believer with an unbeliever?. . .Wherefore:—

Come ye out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord,

And touch no unclean thing;

And I will receive you,

And will be to you a FATHER,

And ye shall be to Me sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty.

We have to make our choice: we cannot enjoy both the world and CHRIST.

The bride had not learned this. She wanted to enjoy both, with no thought that they could not go together. She watches with joy as the Bridegroom approaches.

The voice of my Beloved! Behold He cometh

Leaping upon the mountain, bounding over the hills.

My Beloved is like a gazelle or a young hart;

Behold He standeth behind our wall,

He looketh in at the windows,

He glanceth through the lattice.

The bride’s heart leaps when she hears her Beloved’s voice as He comes looking for her. He has crossed the hills; He comes near her; He stands behind the wall; He even looks in at the windows; with tender, moving words He woos her to come out to Him. He speaks no word of blame, and His loving pleas sink deep into her memory.

My Beloved spake, and said unto me,

Rise up, My love, My fair one, and come away,

For, lo, the winter is past,

The rain is over and gone;

The flowers appear on the earth;

The time of the singing of birds is come,

And the voice of the turtle is heard in our land;

The fig-tree ripeneth her green figs,

And the vines are in blossom,

They give forth their fragrance.

Arise, My love, My fair one, and come away.

All nature responds to the return of summer. Will you, My Bride, not respond to My love?

Arise, My love, My fair one, and come away.

Can such pleading be in vain? Sadly, it can, and it was!

In still more moving words the Bridegroom goes on:—

O My dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the covert of the steep place,

Let Me see thy countenance, let Me hear thy voice!

For sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.

What a wonderful thought, that GOD should want fellowship with us, and that He whose love once made Him the Man of Sorrows may now be made the Man of Joys by the loving devotion of human hearts!

But strong as His love and His desire for His bride are, He can come no further. Where she is now, He can never come. Surely, though, she will go out to Him. Does He not have a claim on her? She feels and enjoys His love; will she let His desire count for nothing? For notice that here it is not the bride longing in vain for her LORD, but the Bridegroom who is looking for her. How sad that He should look in vain!

Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vineyards;

For our vineyards are in blossom,

He goes on. The enemies may be small, but the harm they do is great. A little spray of blossom, so tiny it can hardly be seen, is easily spoiled, and yet the fruitfulness of a whole branch may be destroyed forever by it. And how many little foxes there are! Little compromises with the world; disobedience to the still small voice in little things; little indulgences of the flesh at the cost of duty; little pieces of scheming; doing evil in little things so that good may come; and the beauty and fruitfulness of the vine are sacrificed!

The bride’s response gives a sad picture of how deceitful sin is. Instead of springing up to meet Him, she first comforts her own heart by remembering His faithfulness and her union with Him:—

My Beloved is mine, and I am His:

He feedeth His flock among the lilies.

My position is secure; I have no need to worry about it. He is mine, and I am His, and nothing can change that relationship. I can find Him any time I like; He feeds His flock among the lilies. While the sun of prosperity shines on me, I can safely enjoy myself here without Him. If trial and darkness come, He will certainly not fail me.

Until the day be cool, and the shadows flee away,

Turn, my Beloved, and be Thou like a gazelle or a young hart.

Upon the mountains of Bether.

Careless of His desire, she lightly sends Him away like this, thinking: A little later I can enjoy His love. And the grieved Bridegroom goes away!

Poor foolish bride! She will soon find that the things that once satisfied her can satisfy her no longer, and that it is easier to turn a deaf ear to His tender call than to call back or find her absent LORD.

The day grew cool and the shadows fled away, but He did not come back. Then, in the solemn night, she discovered her mistake. It was dark, and she was alone. Going to bed, she still hoped He would return; she had still not learned that worldliness is an absolute barrier to full communion.

By night on my bed I sought Him whom my soul loveth:

I sought Him, but I found Him not!

She waits and grows weary; His absence becomes unbearable:—

I said, I will rise now, and go about the city,

In the streets and in the broad ways.

I will seek Him whom my soul loveth:

I sought Him, but I found Him not!

How different her position is from what it might have been! Instead of searching for Him alone, desolate and in the dark, she might have gone out with Him in the sunshine, leaning on His arm. When she could no longer say “Nothing between,” she might have exchanged her partial view of her Beloved through the lattice for the joy of His embrace, and of His public acknowledgment of her as His chosen bride!

The watchmen that go about the city found me:

To whom I said, Saw ye Him whom my soul loveth?

It was but a little that I passed from them,

When I found Him whom my soul loveth.

She had now obeyed His command, “Arise, and come away.” Unafraid of disgrace, she was searching for Him in the dark; and when she began to confess her LORD, she soon found Him and was restored to His favour:—

I held Him, and would not let Him go,

Until I had brought Him into my mother’s house,

And into the chamber of her that conceived me.

Jerusalem above is the mother of us all. That is where communion is enjoyed, not in worldly ways or self-willed indulgence.

With communion fully restored, the section closes, as the first did, with the Bridegroom’s loving charge that no one should disturb His bride:—

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem,

By the roes, and by the hinds of the field,

(By all that is loving and beautiful and constant)

That ye stir not up, nor awake My love,

Until she please.

While we live down here, in the world but not of it, may we all find our home in the heavenly places where we are seated together with CHRIST. Sent into the world to bear witness for our MASTER, may we always be strangers there, ready to confess Him as the true object of our soul’s devotion.

How amiable are Thy tabernacles,

O Lord of hosts!

My soul longeth, yea even fainteth for the courts of the Lord;

My heart and my flesh cry out unto the living God,

Blessed are they that dwell in Thy house:

They will be still praising Thee. . .

A day in Thy courts is better than a thousand.

I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God

Than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.

For the Lord God is a Sun and Shield:

The Lord will give grace and glory:

No good thing will He withhold from them that walk uprightly.

O Lord of hosts,

Blessed is the man that trusteth in Thee!

fields.title: Section III
fields.body_html:
The Joy of Unbroken Communion

Song 3:6–5:1

O Jesus, King most wonderful,

Thou Conqueror renown’d.

Thou sweetness most ineffable,

In whom all joys are found!

Thee, Jesus, may our voices bless;

Thee may we love alone;

And ever in our lives express

The image of Thine own.

In Sections I and II we were mainly taken up with the words and experiences of the bride. In marked contrast, in this section our attention is first drawn to the Bridegroom, and then it is from Him that we hear about the bride, as the object of His love and the delight of His heart. The daughters of Jerusalem speak first.

Who is this that cometh up out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke,

Perfumed with myrrh and frankincense,

With all powders of the merchant?

They answer the question themselves:—

King Solomon made himself a car of state

Of the wood of Lebanon.

He made the pillars thereof of silver,

The bottom thereof of gold, the seat of it of purple,

The midst thereof being paved with love (love-gifts).

From the daughters of Jerusalem.

Behold, it is the litter of Solomon;

Threescore mighty men are about it,

Of the mighty men of Israel

They all handle the sword, and are expert in war:

Every man hath his sword upon his thigh,

Because of fear in the night.

The bride is not mentioned in these verses. She is outshone by the grandeur and splendour of her royal Bridegroom, and yet she is enjoying it and sharing in it. The very air is perfumed by the smoke of the incense rising like pillars to the clouds; and everything that guards the Bridegroom’s own position and displays His dignity also guards the bride who travels with Him and shares His glory. The state carriage they sit in is built of fragrant cedar from Lebanon, and the finest gold and silver have been lavished on it. The fragrant wood pictures the beauty of sanctified humanity; the gold reminds us of our Lord’s divine glory; and the silver, of the purity and preciousness of His redeemed and matchless Church. The imperial purple it is lined with tells us of the Gentiles; the daughter of Tyre has been there with her gift. And the love-gifts of the daughters of Jerusalem fit the prophecy, “Even the rich among the people shall entreat thy favour.”

These are the things that catch the attention of the daughters of Jerusalem. But the bride is taken up with the King Himself, and she exclaims:—

Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon,

With the crown wherewith His mother hath crowned Him in the day of His espousals,

And in the day of the gladness of His heart.

The crowned KING is everything to her, and she wants Him to be everything to the daughters of Zion too. She dwells with delight on the gladness of His heart on the day of His wedding, for now she is not taken up with Him for her own sake, but rejoices in His joy at finding His satisfaction in her. Do we cultivate this unselfish desire to be all for JESUS, and to do everything for His pleasure, as much as we should? Or are we aware that we mainly go to Him for our own sake, or at best for the sake of other people? How much prayer begins and ends with the creature, forgetting the privilege of giving joy to the Creator! Yet only when He sees His own love reflected in our unselfish love and devotion to Him can His heart be fully satisfied and pour itself out in precious words of love like these:—

Behold, thou art fair, My love; behold, thou art fair;

Thine eyes are as dove’s behind thy veil;

Thy hair is as a flock of goats,

That lie along the side of Mount Gilead;

Thy teeth are like a flock of ewes that are newly shorn,

Which are come up from the washing.

Which are all of them in pairs,

And none is bereaved among them.

Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet,

And thy speech is comely, etc. (See verses 3-5).

We have already found the explanation of the bride’s beauty: she reflects the beauty of the Bridegroom like a mirror. No wonder He can describe her beauty with satisfaction while she is taken up with Him like this! The lips that speak only of Him are like a thread of scarlet; the mouth, the speech, that has no word about self or for self is beautiful in His sight.

We can well imagine how sweet His words of appreciation and praise were to the bride; but her joy was too deep for words, and she was silent in her love. She would not now think of sending Him away until the day grew cool and the shadows fled away.

Still less does the Bridegroom think of finding His joy apart from His bride. He says:—

Until the day be cool, and the shadows flee away,

I will get Me to the mountain of myrrh,

And to the hill of frankincense.

Separation never comes from His side. He is always ready for communion with a prepared heart, and in this happy communion the bride grows ever fairer and more like her LORD. She is being changed step by step into His image, from one degree of glory to another, by the wonderful working of the HOLY SPIRIT, until the Bridegroom can declare:—

Thou art all fair, My love;

And there is no spot on thee.

And now she is fit for service, and the Bridegroom woos her to it; she will not misrepresent Him now:—

Come with Me from Lebanon, My bride,

With Me from Lebanon;

Look from the top of Amana,

From the top of Senir and Hermon,

From the lions’ dens,

From the mountains of the leopards.

“Come with Me.” It is always so. When our SAVIOUR says, “Go ye therefore and disciple all nations,” He first says, “All power is given unto Me,” and afterward, “Lo, I am with you always.” Or when, as here, He calls His bride to come, it is still “with Me”; and it is in connection with this loving invitation that for the first time He changes the words “My love” for the still more tender ones, “My bride.”

What are lions’ dens when the Lion of the tribe of Judah is with us, or mountains of leopards when He is at our side? “I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me.” On the other hand, it is while she is facing dangers like these and toiling with Him in service that He says:—

Thou hast ravished My heart, My sister, My bride;

Thou hast ravished My heart with one look from thine eyes,

With one chain of thy neck.

Is it not wonderful that our Beloved’s heart can be so captured by the love of someone ready to accept His invitation and go out with Him to rescue the perishing? The marginal reading of the Revised Version is very significant: “Thou hast ravished My heart,” or “Thou hast given me courage.” If the Bridegroom’s heart can be encouraged by the faithfulness and loving companionship of His bride, it is no surprise that we can cheer and encourage one another as we serve together. St. Paul had a steep mountain of difficulty to climb when he was being taken as a prisoner to Rome, not knowing what awaited him there; but when the brothers met him at the Forum of Appius, he thanked God and took courage. May we always strengthen one another’s hands in God like this!

But to go on. The Bridegroom cheers the hard climbs and the steep, dangerous paths with sweet expressions of His love:—

How fair is thy love, My sister, My bride!

How much better is thy love than wine!

And the smell of thine ointments than all manner of spices!

Thy lips, O My bride, drop as the honeycomb:

Honey and milk are under thy tongue;

And the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon.

A garden shut up is My sister, My bride;

A spring shut up, a fountain sealed.

Thy shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with precious fruits;

Henna with spikenard plants,

Spikenard and saffron,

Calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense;

Myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices.

Thou art a fountain of gardens,

A well of living waters,

And flowing streams from Lebanon.

As she works with the Bridegroom to rescue the perishing, the words of her lips are like honey and the honeycomb to Him; and picture is piled on picture to express His satisfaction and joy. She is a garden full of precious fruits and delightful perfumes, but a garden enclosed: the fruit she bears may bless many, but the garden is for Him alone. She is a fountain, but a spring shut up, a fountain sealed. And yet she is also a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters and flowing streams from Lebanon: she brings fruitfulness and refreshment wherever she goes, and yet it is all from Him and for Him.

The bride now speaks for the second time in this section. Her first words were about Him; now her second are for Him. Self is found in neither.

Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south;

Blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out.

Let my Beloved come into His garden,

And eat His precious fruits.

She is ready for anything. The north wind and the south may blow on her garden, if only its spices flow out to delight her Lord with their fragrance. He has called her His garden, a paradise of pomegranates and precious fruits; let Him come into it and eat His precious fruits.

The Bridegroom answers:—

I am come into My garden, My sister, My bride:

I have gathered My myrrh with My spice;

I have eaten My honeycomb with My honey;

I have drunk My wine with My milk.

Now, when she calls, He answers at once. When she is for her LORD alone, He assures her that He finds all His satisfaction in her.

The section ends with the bride’s invitation to His friends and hers, as well as to Him:—

Eat, O friends;

Drink, yea, drink abundantly, O Beloved.

Giving everything to our MASTER, far from lessening our power to give to others, increases both our power and our joy in serving. The disciples’ five loaves and two fish, first given up to the LORD and blessed by Him, were plenty for the hungry crowds, and as they were handed out they grew into a supply from which twelve baskets full of pieces were left over when everyone had eaten their fill.

So in this beautiful section, as we have seen, we have a picture of unbroken communion and its delightful results. May our lives match it! First, one with the KING, then speaking of the KING; the joy of communion leading to fellowship in service, to being all for JESUS, ready for any experience that will fit us for further service, surrendering everything to Him and willing to spend everything for Him. There is no room here for love of the world, because union with CHRIST has filled the heart. There is nothing left to gratify the world, because everything has been sealed and is kept for the MASTER’S use.

Jesus, my life is Thine!

And evermore shall be

Hidden in Thee.

For nothing can untwine

Thy life from mine.

fields.title: Section IV
fields.body_html:
Communion again Broken—Restoration

Song 5:2–6:10.

The fourth section opens with the bride speaking to the daughters of Jerusalem. She tells them of her recent sad experience and begs for their help in her trouble. She has once again lost the presence and comfort of her Bridegroom, this time not by slipping back into worldliness, but by lazy self-indulgence.

We are not told the steps that led to her failure, or how self found a place in her heart again. Perhaps the cause was spiritual pride in what grace had enabled her to achieve. Or, quite possibly, the separation came from a cherished satisfaction in the blessing she had received, rather than in the Blesser Himself. She seems to have been largely unaware of her decline. Taken up with herself and content with herself, she hardly noticed His absence. She was resting, resting alone, never asking where He had gone or what He was doing. More than that, the door of her room was not only shut but bolted, a sign that she neither longed for His return nor expected it.

Yet her heart was not far from Him. There was a music in His voice that woke echoes in her soul that no other voice could have stirred. As far as the world was concerned, she was still “a garden shut up, a fountain sealed.” This time the trap was all the more dangerous and subtle because she did not suspect it at all. Let us look at her story:—

I was asleep, but my heart waked:

It is the voice of my Beloved that knocketh saying,

Open to Me, My sister, My love, My dove, My undefiled:

For My head is filled with dew,

My locks with the drops of the night.

How often the Bridegroom stands outside as a Suitor knocking, as in His letter to the church at Laodicea: “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear My voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with Me.” It is sad that He should be outside a closed door and need to knock; but it is sadder still that He should knock, and knock in vain, at the door of any heart that has become His own. In this case it is not the bride’s position that is wrong; if it were, His word would be as before, “Arise, and come away.” Instead His word now is, “Open to Me, My sister, My love.” It was her condition, her self-satisfaction and love of ease, that shut the door.

His words are very moving: “Open to Me, My sister” (He is the firstborn among many brothers and sisters), “My love” (the object of My heart’s devotion), “My dove” (one who has been given many of the gifts and graces of the HOLY SPIRIT), “My undefiled” (washed, renewed, and cleansed for Me); and He urges her to open by pointing to His own condition:—

My head is filled with dew,

My locks with the drops of the night.

Why is His head wet with dew? Because His heart is a shepherd’s heart. Some of those the FATHER has given Him are wandering on the dark mountains of sin. Many, so very many, have never heard the SHEPHERD’S voice; and many who were once in the fold have wandered away, far from its safe shelter. The heart that can never forget, the love that can never fail, must look for the wandering sheep until the lost one is found: “My FATHER worketh hitherto, and I work.” And will she, who so recently was at His side, who gladly braved the lions’ dens and the leopards’ mountains, leave Him to look for the wandering and the lost alone?

Open to Me, My sister, My love, My dove, My undefiled:

For My head is filled with dew,

My locks with the drops of the night.

We know of no more moving appeal in God’s Word, and the bride’s reply is sad indeed:—

I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on?

I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?

How sadly possible it is to delight in conferences and conventions, to feast on all the good things set before us, and yet not be ready to go out from them into self-denying efforts to rescue the perishing; to delight in the rest of faith while forgetting to fight the good fight of faith; to dwell on the cleansing and purity that faith brings, while giving little thought to the poor souls struggling in the mire of sin. If we can take off our coat when He wants us to keep it on, if we can wash our feet while He is wandering alone on the mountains, is there not a sad lack of fellowship with our LORD?

Finding no response from the slow bride, her

Beloved put in His hand by the hole of the door,

And “her” heart was moved for Him.

But sadly the door was not only latched but bolted, and His attempt to get in was in vain.

I rose up to open to my Beloved;

And my hands dropped with myrrh,

And my fingers with liquid myrrh,

Upon the handles of the bolt.

I opened to my Beloved;

But my Beloved had withdrawn Himself, and was gone.

My soul had failed me when He spake.

When the bride did get up, all too late, she seems to have been more concerned with anointing herself with the liquid myrrh than with quickly welcoming her waiting LORD; more taken up with her own graces than with His desire. She spoke no word of welcome, though her heart sank within her, and the grieved One had gone before she was ready to receive Him. Again, as in the third chapter, she had to go out alone to look for her LORD; and this time what she went through was much more painful than before.

I sought Him, but I could not find Him;

I called Him, but He gave me no answer.

The watchmen that go about the city found me,

They smote me, they wounded me;

The keepers of the walls took away my mantle from me.

Her first lapse came from inexperience. If a second lapse came about through carelessness, she should at least have been ready and quick to obey when called. Falling into the habit of being slow to obey is no small thing, even for a believer; for the unbeliever, the final outcome of disobedience is more terrible than words can say:—

Turn you at My reproof:

Behold, I will pour out My Spirit unto you,

I will make known My words unto you.

Because I have called, and ye refused;

I have stretched out My hand, and no man regarded;. . .

I also will laugh in the day of your calamity. . .

Then shall they call upon Me, but I will not answer;

They shall seek Me diligently, but they shall not find Me.

The bride’s backsliding, though painful, was not final, because true repentance followed. She went out into the darkness and looked for Him. She called, but He did not answer, and the watchmen who found her struck her and wounded her. They seem to have understood how serious her decline was better than she had. Believers may be blind to their own inconsistencies, but others notice them; and the closer our place to our LORD, the more surely any failure will bring reproach.

Wounded, disgraced, unsuccessful in her search and close to despair, the bride turns to the daughters of Jerusalem. Telling them the story of her sorrows, she charges them to tell her Beloved that she is not unfaithful to Him or forgetful of Him.

I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my Beloved,

That ye tell Him, that I am sick of love.

The daughters of Jerusalem’s reply shows very clearly that the grief-stricken bride, wandering in the dark, is not recognized as the KING’S bride, though her personal beauty does not go unnoticed.

What is thy Beloved more than another beloved,

O thou fairest among women?

What is thy Beloved more than another beloved,

That thou dost so adjure us?

This question, which suggests that her Beloved is no more than anyone else, stirs her soul to its depths. Forgetting herself, she pours out from the fullness of her heart an enchanting description of her LORD’S glory and beauty.

My Beloved is white and ruddy,

The chiefest among ten thousand.

(see verses 10–16, ending with)

His mouth is most sweet; yea, He is altogether lovely.

This is my Beloved, and this is my Friend,

O daughters of Jerusalem.

It is interesting to compare the bride’s description of the Bridegroom with the descriptions of “the Ancient of Days” in Daniel 7:9–10 and of our risen LORD in Revelation 1:13–16. The differences are very telling.

In Daniel 7 we see the Ancient of Days seated on the throne of judgment. His clothing was white as snow and the hair of His head like pure wool; His throne and its wheels were like burning fire, and a river of fire flowed out from before Him. The Son of Man was brought before Him and received from Him dominion and glory and an everlasting kingdom that will never be destroyed. In Revelation 1 we see the Son of Man Himself, clothed in a robe reaching to His feet, and His head and hair were white as wool, white as snow. But the bride sees her Bridegroom in all the vigour of youth, with locks “bushy, and black as a raven.” The risen SAVIOUR’S eyes are described as “a flame of fire,” but His bride sees them “like doves beside the water brooks.” In Revelation “His voice is as the voice of many waters. . .and out of His mouth proceeded a sharp two-edged sword.” To the bride, His lips are like lilies dripping liquid myrrh, and His mouth is most sweet. The risen SAVIOUR’S face was “as the sun shineth in his strength,” and the effect of the vision on John, “when I saw Him, I fell at His feet as one dead,” was much like the effect of the vision given to Saul as he came near Damascus. But to His bride, “His aspect is like Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.” The LION of the tribe of Judah is, to His own bride, the KING of love. With a full heart and a shining face she describes His beauties in such a way that the daughters of Jerusalem are seized with a strong desire to look for Him with her, so that they too may see His beauty.

Whither is thy Beloved gone,

O thou fairest among women?

Whither hath thy Beloved turned Him,

That we may seek Him with thee?

The bride answers:—

My Beloved is gone down to His garden, to the beds of spices,

To feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies.

I am my Beloved’s, and my Beloved is mine:

He feedeth His flock among the lilies.

Forlorn and desolate as she might look, she still knows she is the object of His love, and she claims Him as her own. This expression, “I am my Beloved’s, and my Beloved is mine,” is like the one in the second chapter, “My Beloved is mine, and I am His,” and yet there is a notable difference. Then her first thought about CHRIST was of her claim on Him, and His claim on her came second. Now she thinks first of His claim, and only afterward mentions her own. We see grace grow further still in chapter 7:10, where the bride loses sight of her own claim altogether and says:—

I am my Beloved’s,

And His desire is toward me.

No sooner has she said these words, and acknowledged herself as His rightful possession (a claim she had in practice rejected when she kept Him bolted out), than her Bridegroom Himself appears. With no word of blame, but with the tenderest love, He tells her how beautiful she is in His eyes, and speaks her praise to the daughters of Jerusalem.

To her, He says:—

Thou art beautiful, O My love, as Tirzah,

(the beautiful city of Samaria,)

Comely as Jerusalem,

(the glorious city of the great King,)

Terrible (or rather brilliant) as an army with banners.

Turn away thine eyes from Me,

For they have overcome Me. (See vv. 4-7).

Then, turning to the daughters of Jerusalem, He exclaims:—

There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines,

And maidens without number.

My dove, My perfect one, is but one;

She is the only one of her mother;

She is the choice one of her that bare her.

The daughters saw her, and called her blessed;

Yea, the queens and the concubines, and they praised her, saying,

Who is she that looketh forth as the morning,

Fair as the moon,

Clear as the sun,

Brilliant as an army with banners?

So the section closes with communion fully restored: the bride is reinstated and openly acknowledged by the Bridegroom as His own matchless companion and friend. The painful experience the bride has been through has brought lasting good. We see no further sign of broken communion; in the remaining sections there is only joy and fruitfulness.

fields.title: Section V
fields.body_html:
Fruits of Recognized Union

Song 6:11–8:4.

In the second and fourth sections of this book we found the bride’s communion broken: in the second by backsliding into worldliness, and in the fourth through lazy ease and self-satisfaction. This section, like the third, is one of unbroken communion. It opens with the bride’s words:—

I went down into the garden of nuts,

To see the green plants of the valley

To see whether the vine budded.

And the pomegranates were in flower.

Or ever I was aware, my soul set me

Among the chariots of my willing people.

At the start of Section III the bride, in unbroken communion with her LORD, was present though not mentioned, until she made her presence known by speaking to the daughters of Zion. In the same way, in this section the KING’S presence goes unnoticed until He Himself speaks to His bride. But she is one with her LORD as she goes about His service! His promise, “Lo, I am with you alway,” is always fulfilled for her. He no longer needs to woo her to arise and come away, to tell her that His “head is filled with dew,” His “locks with the drops of the night,” or to urge her, if she loves Him, to feed His sheep and care for His lambs. She is His garden herself, and she does not forget to tend it, or keep other people’s vineyards while her own is neglected. With Him as well as for Him, she goes to the garden of nuts. So complete is the union between them that many commentators have found it hard to decide whether the bride or the Bridegroom is speaking, and really it matters little; for, as we have said, both were there, and of one mind. Still, we believe we are right to give these words to the bride, since she is the one the daughters of Jerusalem address, and the one who answers them.

It seems their willing people found the bride and Bridegroom while they were engaged in this happy fellowship of fruitful service, and before she knew it the bride found herself seated among the chariots of her people: her people as well as His.

The daughters of Jerusalem would like to call her back:—

Return, return, O Shulammite;

Return, return, that we may look upon thee.

There is no question now about who she is, or why her Beloved is more than any other. He is recognized as King Solomon, and she is given the same name, only in its feminine form (Shulammite).

Some have seen in these words, “Return, return,” a hint of the rapture of the Church, and explain some later parts of the passage that seem to conflict with this view as looking ahead rather than moving forward in sequence. Interesting as the idea is, and well as it would explain why the KING is not mentioned in the verses before, we are not inclined to accept it. We see the whole song as moving forward, and its last words as matching the closing words of the Book of Revelation, “Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, LORD JESUS.” So we do not regard the bride’s leaving her garden as anything but temporary.

The bride answers the daughters of Jerusalem:—

Why will ye look upon the Shulammite?

or, as in the Authorized Version,

What will ye see in the Shulammite?

In the KING’S presence she cannot imagine why anyone should pay attention to her. Just as Moses, coming down from the mountain, did not know that his face shone with a divine glory, so it was with the bride. But we can learn this very important lesson: many who do not see the beauty of the LORD will not fail to admire His beauty reflected in His bride. The eager gaze of the daughters of Jerusalem surprised the bride, and she says, You might be looking “upon the dance of Mahanaim,” the dance of two companies of Israel’s fairest daughters, instead of at one who has no claim on anyone’s attention except that she is the chosen, though unworthy, bride of the glorious KING.

The daughters of Jerusalem have no trouble answering her question. Recognizing her as royal by birth, “O Prince’s daughter,” as well as queenly in dignity, they describe in true Eastern language the tenfold beauties of her person; from her feet to her head they see only beauty and perfection. What a contrast to her natural state! Once, “from the sole of the foot even unto the head,” there was “but wounds, and bruises, and festering sores.” Now her feet are “shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace,” and the very hair of her head shows her to be a Nazarite indeed; “the KING” Himself “is held captive in the tresses thereof.”

But One who means more to her than the daughters of Jerusalem answered her simple question, “What will ye see in the Shulamite?” The Bridegroom Himself replies:—

How fair and how pleasant art thou,

O love, for delights!

He sees in her the beauty and fruitfulness of the tall, upright palm, of the graceful, clinging vine, and of the fragrant, evergreen citron. Grace has made her like the palm tree, the emblem of both uprightness and fruitfulness. The Eastern traveller values the fruit of the date palm more than bread, because it sustains so well; and the tree does not lose its power to bear fruit. As it grows older, its fruit becomes more perfect as well as more plentiful.

The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree:

He shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.

They that are planted in the house of the Lord

Shall flourish in the courts of our God.

They shall still bring forth fruit in old age;

They shall be full of sap and green.

But why are the righteous made so upright and flourishing?

To show that the Lord is upright;

He is my Rock, and there is no unrighteousness in Him.

One with our LORD, it is our part to show His graces and virtues, to reflect His beauty, and to be His faithful witnesses.

The palm is also the emblem of victory. It lifts its beautiful crown toward the heavens, unafraid of the heat of the sultry sun or the burning wind from the desert. Because of its beauty it was one of the ornaments of Solomon’s temple, as it is to be of Ezekiel’s. When our SAVIOUR was welcomed at Jerusalem as the KING of Israel, the people took palm branches and went out to meet Him. And on the glorious day of His wedding, “a great multitude, which no man” can “number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues,” will stand “before the throne and before the LAMB, clothed with white robes”; and with palms of victory in their hands they will give their “salvation to our GOD which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the LAMB.”

But if she is like the palm, she is also like the vine. She badly needs the Gardener’s care, and she repays it well. Abiding in CHRIST, the true source of fruitfulness, she brings forth clusters of grapes, juicy and refreshing as well as sustaining, like the fruit of the palm: juicy and refreshing to Him, the owner of the vineyard, and also to the weary, thirsty world He has placed it in.

The vine has its own lessons to teach. It needs support and looks for it. The pruner’s sharp knife often cuts away its tender garlands without mercy and spoils its appearance, while making it more fruitful. It has been beautifully written:—

The living Vine, Christ chose it for Himself:—

God gave to man for use and sustenance

Corn, wine, and oil, and each of these is good:

And Christ is Bread of life and Light of life.

But yet, He did not choose the summer corn,

That shoots up straight and free in one quick growth,

And has its day, is done, and springs no more;

Nor yet the olive, all whose boughs are spread

In the soft air, and never lose a leaf,

Flowering and fruitful in perpetual peace;

But only this, for Him and His is one,—

That everlasting, ever-quickening Vine,

That gives the heat and passion of the world,

Through its own life-blood, still renewed and shed.

* * * * * * *

The Vine from every living limb bleeds wine;

Is it the poorer for that spirit shed?

The drunkard and the wanton drink thereof;

Are they the richer for that gift’s excess?

Measure thy life by loss instead of gain;

Not by the wine drunk, but the wine poured forth;

For love’s strength standeth in love’s sacrifice;

And whoso suffers most, hath most to give.

The Bridegroom uses one more picture: “The smell of thy breath (is) like apples,” or rather citrons. In the first section the bride exclaims:—

As the citron-tree among the trees of the wood,

So is my Beloved among the sons.

I delighted and sat down under His shadow,

And His fruit was sweet to my taste.

Here we see the result of that communion. The citrons she had fed on perfumed her breath and gave her their delicious scent. The Bridegroom ends His description:—

Thy mouth (is) like the best wine,

That goeth down smoothly—

For my Beloved—

interjects the bride,

Causing the lips of those that are asleep to move.

How wonderful the grace that has made the bride of CHRIST all this to her Beloved! Upright as the palm, victorious, and ever more fruitful as she grows heavenward; gentle and tender as the Vine, self-forgetful and self-sacrificing, bearing fruit not just in spite of hardship but bearing her richest fruit through it; feasting on her Beloved as she rests in His shade, and so sharing His fragrance: what has grace not done for her! And what joy she must have in finding, ever more fully, that the glorious Bridegroom is satisfied in the lowly wild flower He has made His bride and made beautiful with His own graces and virtues!

I am my Beloved’s,

And His desire is toward me,

she gladly exclaims. Now there is nothing of self or for self; it is all of You and for You. And if such sweet fruit comes from going down to the garden of nuts and caring for His garden with Him, she will need no urging to carry on in this blessed service.

Come, my Beloved, let us go forth into the field;

Let us lodge in the villages.

She is not ashamed of her humble origin, because she fears no shame: perfect love has cast out fear. The King’s royal state, with its pomp and grandeur, can be enjoyed later. For now it is sweeter to have Him at her side making the garden fruitful; to give Him all kinds of precious fruits, new and old, which she has stored up for Him; and best of all, to satisfy Him with her own love. She is not only content with this fellowship of service; she could almost wish there were no honours and duties to claim His attention and, for the moment, lessen the joy of His presence.

Oh that Thou wert as my brother,

That sucked the breasts of my mother!

When I should find Thee without, I would kiss Thee;

Yea, and none would despise me.

If only she could care for Him and have His whole attention, as a sister might care for a brother. She is deeply aware that He has given her rich gifts, and that she is nothing compared with Him. But instead of proudly dwelling on what she has done through Him, she wishes it were possible for her to be the giver and Him the receiver. How far this is from the grudging thought that must so grate on our LORD’S heart: “I do not think that GOD requires this of me,” or, “Must I give up that, if I am to be a Christian?” True devotion will rather ask to be allowed to give, and will count as loss everything that cannot be given up for the LORD’S sake: “I count all things but loss, for the excellency of the knowledge of CHRIST JESUS my LORD.”

This longing to be more to Him does not, however, blind her to the fact that she needs His guidance, and that He is her true and only Teacher.

I would lead Thee, and bring Thee into my mother’s house,

That Thou mightest instruct me;

I would cause Thee to drink of spiced wine,

Of the juice of my pomegranate.

I would give You my best, and yet I would look for all my own rest and satisfaction in You.

His left hand should be under my head,

And His right hand should embrace me.

And so the section ends. Nothing is sweeter to the Bridegroom or to the bride than this holy, unhindered communion; and again He charges the daughters of Jerusalem, in a slightly different form:—

Why should ye stir up, or why awake My love,

Until she please?

Holy communion indeed! May we always enjoy it; and abiding in CHRIST, we will sing, in the familiar words of the well-known hymn—

Both Thine arms are clasped around me,

And my head is on Thy breast;

And my weary soul hath found Thee

Such a perfect, perfect rest!

Blessed Jesus,

Now I know that I am blest.

fields.title: Section VI
fields.body_html:
Unrestrained Communion

Cant. viii. 5-14.

We have now reached the last section of this book, which, as we have seen, is a poem describing the life of a believer on earth. It begins in Section I (Song 1:2–2:7) with the unsatisfied longings of a betrothed woman, longings that could only be met by her complete surrender to the Bridegroom of her soul. When the surrender was made, instead of the cross she had feared so much she found a King, the KING of LOVE, who both satisfied her deepest longings and found His own satisfaction in her.

The second section (Song 2:8–3:5) showed failure on her part. She was lured back into the world and soon found that her Beloved could not follow her there. Then, going out with her whole heart to look for Him and confessing His name, she found Him, and her communion was restored.

The third section (Song 3:6–5:1) told of unbroken communion. Abiding in Christ, she shared His security and His glory. Yet she turns the attention of the daughters of Jerusalem away from these outward things to her KING Himself. And while she is taken up with Him, and wants others to be taken up with Him too, she finds that her royal Bridegroom delights in her and invites her into fellowship in service, unafraid of lions’ dens and leopards’ mountains.

The fourth section (Song 5:2–6:10), however, shows failure again, not through worldliness as before, but through spiritual pride and laziness. This time restoration was much harder. But again, when she went out earnestly to look for her LORD, and confessed Him in such a way that others longed to find Him with her, He revealed Himself, and communion was restored, never to be broken again.

The fifth section (Song 6:11–8:4), as we have seen, describes not only the shared satisfaction and delight of the bride and Bridegroom in each other, but also the daughters of Jerusalem’s recognition of her position and her beauty.

And now in the sixth section (Song 8:5–14) we come to the closing scene of the book. In it the bride is seen leaning on her Beloved, asking Him to bind her even more firmly to Himself, and busy in His vineyard until He calls her away from earthly service. We will now look at this last section more closely.

Like the third, it opens with a question or exclamation from the daughters of Jerusalem. There they asked, “Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, etc.?” But then their attention was caught by the pomp and splendour of the KING, not by His person or by His bride. Here they are drawn by the bride’s happy position in relation to her Beloved, and not by their surroundings.

Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness,

Leaning upon her Beloved?

It is through the bride that attention is drawn to the Bridegroom; their union and communion are now open and plain to see. The wilderness is mentioned for the last time, but sweetly comforted by the Bridegroom’s presence, it is no wilderness to this bride. With all the trust of confident love she is seen leaning on her Beloved. He is her strength, her joy, her pride and her prize, while she is His special treasure, the object of His tenderest care. All His resources of wisdom and power are hers. Though she is travelling, she is at rest; though in the wilderness, she is satisfied, as she leans on her Beloved.

Wonderful as the revelations of grace and love are that the HOLY SPIRIT teaches the heart through the relationship of bride and Bridegroom, the CHRIST of GOD is more than a Bridegroom to His people. He who could say on earth, “Before Abraham was, I am,” here claims His bride from her very birth, and not only from her betrothal. Before she knew Him, He knew her; and He reminds her of this in the words:—

I raised thee up under the citron-tree;
