There thy mother brought thee forth.

He delights in her beauty, but that is not so much the cause of His love as its effect; for He took her up when she had no beauty at all. The love that has made her what she is, and now delights in her, is not a fickle love, and she need not fear that it will change.

The bride gladly recognizes the truth that she is indeed His own, and she exclaims:

Set me as a seal upon Thine heart, as a seal upon Thine arm:

For love is strong as death;

Jealousy (ardent love) is cruel (retentive) as the grave;

The flashes thereof are flashes of fire,

A very flame of the Lord.

The High Priest carried the names of the twelve tribes over his heart, each name engraved like a seal on the costly, imperishable stone God had chosen, and each seal or stone set in the purest gold. He also carried the same names on his shoulders, showing that both the love and the strength of the High Priest were pledged on behalf of the tribes of Israel. The bride wants to be carried in this way by the One who is her Prophet, Priest and King, for love is strong as death, and jealousy, or ardent love, holds on as fast as the grave. It is not that she doubts her Beloved’s faithfulness, but that she has learned, sadly, how unfaithful her own heart is; and she wants to be bound to her Beloved’s heart and arm with chains and settings of gold, always the emblem of divinity. So the Psalmist prayed, “Bind the sacrifice with cords, even unto the horns of the altar.”

It is fairly easy to lay the sacrifice on the altar that sanctifies the gift, but it takes divine constraint, the cords of love, to keep it there. So here the bride wants to be set and fixed on the heart and the arm of the One who is from now on to be her all in all, so that she may always trust only in that love and be sustained only by that power.

Do we not all need to learn a lesson from this, and pray to be kept from turning to Egypt for help, from trusting in horses and chariots, from putting our confidence in princes or in mortal men rather than in the living GOD? How often the kings of Israel, who had won great victories by faith, turned aside to heathen nations in their later years! May the LORD keep His people from this trap.

The bride goes on: “The flashes of love are flashes of fire, a very flame of the LORD.” It is worth noting that this is the only place in this book where the word “LORD” appears. But how could it be left out here? For love is of GOD, and GOD is love.

To her request the Bridegroom replies with reassuring words:

Many waters cannot quench love,

Neither can the floods drown it:

If a man would give all the substance of his house for love,

It would utterly be condemned.

The love that grace has brought to life in the bride’s heart is itself divine and enduring. Many waters cannot quench it, nor can floods drown it. Suffering and pain, bereavement and loss may test how constant it is, but they will not quench it. Its source is not human or natural; like the fire, it is hidden with CHRIST in GOD. What “shall separate us from the love of CHRIST? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?. . .Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors, through Him that loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creation (R.V. margin), shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in CHRIST JESUS our LORD.” Our love for GOD is made secure by GOD’S love for us. For the soul truly rescued by grace, no bribe to abandon GOD’S love will succeed in the end. “If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be condemned.”

Free from worry about herself, the happy bride next asks for guidance and fellowship in service with her LORD on behalf of those who have not yet reached her favoured position.

We have a little sister,

And she hath no breasts:

What shall we do for our sister

In the day when she shall be spoken for?

How beautifully her awareness of her union with the Bridegroom shows in her words. “We have a little sister,” not I have; “what shall we do for our sister?” She no longer has any private relationships or interests; in everything she is one with Him. And we see grace grow further in the very question. Toward the end of the last section she recognized the Bridegroom as her Teacher. Now she will not make her own plans for her little sister and then ask Him to agree to them. She would rather learn what His thoughts are and share with Him in His plans.

How much worry and care God’s children would be spared if they learned to act like this! Is it not all too common to make the best plans we can, carry them out as best we can, feel a great weight of responsibility the whole time, and earnestly ask the LORD to help us? But if we always let Him be our Teacher in service and left the responsibility with Him, our strength would not be drained by worry and anxiety; it would all be at His disposal and accomplish His purposes.

In the little sister, still immature, may we not see God’s chosen ones, given to CHRIST in God’s purpose but not yet brought into a saving relationship with Him? And perhaps also those babies in CHRIST who still need to be fed with milk rather than solid food, but who, with such care, will in time become experienced believers, fit for the LORD’S service? Then they will be spoken for, and called into the area of service He has prepared them for.

The Bridegroom answers:—

If she be a wall,

We will build upon her battlements of silver;

And if she be a door,

We will enclose her with boards of cedar.

In this reply the Bridegroom sweetly acknowledges His oneness with His bride, just as she has shown her awareness of her oneness with Him. As she says, “What shall we do for our sister?” so He replies, “We will build . . . we will enclose.” He will not carry out His purposes of grace without His bride, but will work with her and through her. What can be done for this sister, however, will depend on what she becomes. If she is a wall, built on the true foundation, strong and stable, she will be adorned and made beautiful with battlements of silver. But if she is unstable and easily swung back and forth like a door, such treatment would be as impossible as it would be unsuitable; she will need to be enclosed with boards of cedar, hedged in with restraints, for her own protection.

The bride answers joyfully, “I am a wall.” She knows the foundation she is built on; there is no “if” in her case. She knows she has found favour in her Beloved’s eyes. Naphtali’s blessing is hers: she is “satisfied with favour, and full with the blessing of the LORD.”

But what does the link between this happy awareness and the lines that follow teach us?

Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon;

He let out the vineyard unto keepers;

Every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver.

My vineyard, which is mine, is before me;

Thou, O Solomon, shalt have the thousand,

And those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred.

The link is, we believe, very important. It teaches us that what she was (by grace) mattered more than what she did, and that she did not work in order to earn favour; being sure of favour, she let her love show itself freely in service. The bride knew her relationship to her LORD and His love for her. In her resolve that He should have the thousand pieces of silver, her concern was that her vineyard should not produce less for her Solomon than His vineyard at Baal-hamon. Her vineyard was herself, and she wanted much fruit for her LORD. She would also see to it that the keepers of the vineyard, her companions in tending it, who served in word and doctrine, were well rewarded. She would not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. A full tithe, indeed a double tithe, was to be the share of those who kept the fruit and worked with her in the vineyard.

How long this happy service goes on, and how soon it will end, we cannot tell. He who calls His servants to live in the gardens and tend them for Him, as Adam long ago was placed in God’s paradise, alone knows the limit of this service. Sooner or later the rest will come. The burden and heat of the last day will have been borne, the last battle will be over, and the Bridegroom’s voice will be heard speaking to His loved one:—

Thou that dwellest in the gardens,

The companions hearken to thy voice:

Cause Me to hear it.

Your service among the companions is finished. You have fought the good fight, you have kept the faith, you have finished your course; from now on there is laid up for you the crown of righteousness, and the Bridegroom Himself will be your exceeding great reward!

Well may the bride let Him hear her voice, and, her heart leaping out to meet Him, cry:—

Make haste, my Beloved,

And be Thou like to a roe or to a young hart

Upon the mountains of spices!

She no longer asks Him, as in the second section:—

Turn, my Beloved, and be Thou like a roe or a young hart

Upon the mountains of Bether (separation).

She has never again wanted Him to turn away from her, because there are no mountains of Bether for those who are abiding in CHRIST; now there are mountains of spices. He who lives among the praises of Israel, which rise like the incense of spices from His people’s hearts, is invited by His bride to hurry, to come quickly, and to be like a roe or a young hart on the mountains of spices.

The presence of our LORD is very sweet as He lives among His people by His SPIRIT while they serve Him here below. But here there are many thorns on every path that call for watchful care, and it is right that for now we should suffer with our LORD, so that afterward we may be glorified together. Soon, though, the day is coming when He will bring us up out of the earthly gardens and their associations to the palace of the great KING. There His people “shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat. For the LAMB, which is in the midst of the throne, shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters; and GOD shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.”

The SPIRIT and the bride say, Come!. . .

Surely I come quickly.

Amen; even so, come, LORD JESUS!

fields.title: Appendix
fields.body_html:
The Daughters of Jerusalem

People often ask, Who do the daughters of Jerusalem represent?

They are clearly not the bride, yet they are not far from her. They know where the Bridegroom makes His flock rest at noon. The Bridegroom charges them not to stir up or awaken His love while she rests, abiding in Him. They draw attention to the Bridegroom as He comes up from the wilderness with dignity and splendour; their love-gifts adorn His state carriage. The bride appeals to them for help in finding her Beloved, and, stirred by her passionate description of His beauty, they want to look for Him with her. They describe the bride’s beauty very fully. But on the other hand, we never find them taken up with the person of the Bridegroom. He is not all in all to them; their minds are on outward and earthly things.

Do they not represent those who, if not actually saved, are very close to it; or, if saved, are only half-saved? People who for now care more about the things of this world than the things of GOD? Advancing their own interests and securing their own comfort matters more to them than pleasing the LORD in everything. They may be part of that great company spoken of in Revelation 7:9–17, who come out of the great tribulation, but they will not be part of the 144,000, “the first-fruits unto GOD and to the LAMB” (Revelation 14:1–5). They have forgotten our LORD’S warning in Luke 21:34–36, and so they are not “accounted worthy to escape all these things that shall come to pass, and to stand before the SON of Man.” They have not, with Paul, counted “all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of CHRIST JESUS the LORD,” and so they do not “attain unto” that resurrection from among the dead, which Paul felt he might miss but aimed to reach.

We want to put on record our solemn conviction that not all who are Christians, or think they are, will reach the resurrection St Paul speaks of in Philippians 3:11, or will meet the LORD in the air in this way. To those who show by lives of consecration that they are not of the world, but are looking for Him, “He will appear without sin unto salvation.”
